articles.title: One issue, many stories

body.support:
When something is an **issue**, it shows up everywhere. It's in the news, in posts and in ads. Each text tells it differently.

**Different texts, different jobs**

- A **news report** tells you what happened. It should give facts and more than one side.
- An **opinion column** gives one view.
- A **post or video** is short. It wants you to react or share.
- An **ad** wants you to do something.

**How to compare.** Ask the same questions about each text:

1. What does it want me to think or do?
2. Who is it for?
3. What's the main idea?
4. What **evidence** does it give?
5. Are the words and pictures loaded?
6. What's left out?

Put your notes in a table.

**Then have your say.** Decide what you think. Back it with the best evidence.

- *I think… because…*
- *The best evidence is…*

No one text tells the whole story. Compare them to get closer.
body.core:
When something becomes an **issue**, it shows up everywhere: in the news, in opinion columns, in posts and videos, in ads, and in statements from councils and companies. Each kind of text tells the story differently.

**Different texts, different jobs**

- A **news report** aims to inform. It should quote sources, give facts, and include more than one side.
- An **opinion column** argues one **point of view**. It picks the evidence that helps its case.
- A **social media post or video** is short and fast. It often aims to make you react, share or join in.
- An **ad or campaign** wants you to do something: buy, vote, donate, sign.
- An **official statement** gives an organisation's side, often with key facts.

**How to compare.** Put the texts side by side and ask the same questions of each:

1. **Purpose:** what does it want me to think or do?
2. **Audience:** who is it for?
3. **Main idea:** what's the most important point?
4. **Evidence:** what facts, numbers or quotes back it up?
5. **Words and pictures:** are they neutral, or loaded?
6. **What's left out:** whose voice or which facts are missing?

Take notes in a table, so you can see the **contrasts** at a glance.

**Then have your say.** Once you've compared the coverage, you can form your own **point of view**. Back it with the best evidence you found, not just the loudest voice.

- *I think… because…*
- *The strongest evidence is…*
- *Some people argue… but…*

No single text gives you the whole story. Comparing them is how you get close.
body.extend:
When a topic becomes an **issue**, it travels through many text types at once: news reports, opinion columns, social media posts and videos, advertising campaigns, and official statements. Each **frames** the issue differently.

**Text types and their purposes**

- **News reports** aim to inform. They should attribute claims, give facts and include several perspectives.
- **Opinion columns** argue a **point of view**, choosing evidence that supports it.
- **Social media posts and videos** are brief and fast. They often seek a reaction: a share, a like, a sign-up.
- **Ads and campaigns** aim for action: buy, vote, donate, sign.
- **Official statements** present an organisation's position, often with key facts.

**A framework for comparison.** Apply the same lenses to each text:

1. **Purpose:** what's the intended effect?
2. **Audience:** who is it aimed at?
3. **Main idea:** what's the central claim?
4. **Evidence:** what supports it, and is it reliable?
5. **Language and visuals:** are they neutral or loaded? How do they position the reader?
6. **Omissions:** which voices or facts are missing?

Record your notes in a table so the **contrasts** are easy to see.

**Forming a view.** Comparison is the basis for your own **point of view**. Support it with the strongest, most reliable evidence. Then acknowledge other views: *Some argue… however…*

No single text tells the whole story. Comparing coverage is how an informed reader gets close to it.

caseStudies.title: Where Australians get their news

body.support:
Each year, the **University of Canberra** asks Australians where they get their news.

In **2025**, it found:

- **TV** was still the top place for news. **37%** of people said so.
- For the **first time**, more people got their news mainly from **social media** (**26%**) than from **news websites** (**23%**).
- Only **24%** had been taught how to check the news.

On social media, news is mixed in with ads, jokes and opinions. They can all look the same.

So you need to work out what kind of text it is, and what it wants.
body.core:
Each year, the **University of Canberra** runs a big survey called the **Digital News Report: Australia**. It asks Australians where they get their news, and what they think of it.

The **2025** report, released in June 2025, found a big change.

- **TV** was still the most common main source of news, for **37%** of people.
- But for the **first time**, more people named **social media** as their main source (**26%**) than **news websites** (**23%**).
- Only **24%** said they had ever been taught **news literacy**: how to check and make sense of the news.

That matters. On social media, news is mixed in with opinions, ads, jokes and posts from friends. A news report, an opinion and a campaign video can all appear one after another, and look much the same.

So it's up to each reader to work out what kind of text they're looking at, what it wants, and whether it's telling the whole story.
body.extend:
The **Digital News Report: Australia** is an annual survey by the **University of Canberra**'s News and Media Research Centre. It tracks where Australians get news and how they view it.

The **2025** report, released in June 2025, recorded a shift.

- **Television** remained the most common main source of news (**37%**).
- For the **first time**, **social media** (**26%**) overtook **online news websites** (**23%**) as a main source.
- Only **24%** of respondents said they had received any **news literacy** education.

The shift has consequences for readers. In a social feed, news reports, opinion pieces, sponsored posts, campaign videos and jokes appear side by side, often in similar formats. The cues that once separated them, such as the front page versus the opinion page, are weaker.

That places more responsibility on audiences to identify each text's type, purpose and reliability, and to compare sources before forming a view.

model.text:
**The issue:** Should e-scooters be allowed on footpaths?

**Text 1: a news report.** It gives both sides and quotes the police and a rider. The words are neutral.

**Text 2: an opinion column.** It is one-sided. It says scooters are “a menace”. It tells one story about an injury and gives no numbers.

**Text 3: a scooter company's post.** It only shows the benefits. It wants to sell rides.

**My view:** Scooters should stay off busy footpaths. The news report quoted hospital figures. That is the strongest evidence, because it does not come from someone with something to sell.

teacher.overview: The Issues & Voices boss level. Students compare how news reports, opinion columns, social posts, ads and official statements present the same issue, using six lenses: purpose, audience, main idea, evidence, language and visuals, and what's left out. They annotate and compare three made-up texts about a youth centre, then choose a real issue, take notes on three different text types, write a comparison and a supported point of view, and share it in a small group. The case study is the Digital News Report: Australia 2025, which found that social media (26%) overtook news websites (23%) as a main source of news for the first time.
prep: Prepare a list of real, current issues with coverage across text types (e.g. a local council decision, school phone rules, a sports decision, the social media minimum age).
Check students can access news sites on school devices (some have paywalls; ABC, SBS and The Conversation are free).
Model one comparison with a real issue before the final mission.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** a news report informs with facts, sources and several sides; an opinion column argues one view with selected evidence. Purpose, audience, main idea, evidence, words and pictures, what's left out. With the best, most reliable evidence (and by acknowledging other views).

**Three texts:** 1 neutral headline; 2 facts (cost) and both sides; 3 loaded headline (“waste”); 4 emotive words, no evidence; 5 call to action aimed at young people; 6 positive image.

**Compare (suggested):** audience: local residents / ratepayers who read the paper / young people on social media; main idea: council will vote on a $3.2m centre / it's a waste while roads are poor / young people deserve somewhere to go; evidence: cost, both views / none, just claims / none, just feeling and image; words and pictures: neutral / loaded (waste, playground) / emotive, emoji, bright photo; left out: (little) / young people's view, benefits / cost and parking concerns.

**Case study:** TV 37% main source; social media 26% overtook news websites 23% for the first time; 24% had news literacy education. On social media, news, opinion, ads and jokes look alike, so readers must work out what each text is and wants.

realityCheck: **Finding three text types takes time.** Pre-select issues with coverage across types, especially for support students.
**Paywalls get in the way.** Point students to free outlets.
**Keep it balanced.** Students should apply the same lenses to texts they agree with.
**Writing can stall.** The starters and a modelled paragraph help a lot.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It sets up Have Your Say, where students argue their own view out loud.

levels.extend: Adds contrast and frame to the vocabulary, a quiz question on visuals, framing and omissions, responding to an opposing view, and Level Ups on language and visuals.
